newsitem.title: USA: Alleged Nazi guard wounded by Kansas police.
newsitem.headline: Alleged Nazi guard wounded by Kansas police.

text.p: An alleged former Nazi concentration camp guard being investigated by U.S. federal authorities was shot and wounded on Tuesday after firing gunshots at police as reporters looked on, police said.
The leg wound sustained by Michael Kolnhofer, 79, was not life-threatening, Kansas City, Kansas, police spokesman Don Denny said, and he was taken to a hospital.
The confrontation began on Tuesday afternoon when reporters descended on Kolnhofer's modest suburban home after the Justice Department said it had begun proceedings to revoke his U.S. citizenship.

Denny said Kolnhofer brandished a gun and told reporters to leave him alone and to call his lawyer. He then fired at police when they arrived and was wounded in the leg when police returned fire, collapsing on his front porch.
"The guy comes out of his house wielding a gun and telling people to leave. The police showed up and the man fired several shots at the officers. Fortunately, he didn't hit anybody," Denny said.

In a news release issued earlier, the Justice Department's Nazi-hunting Office of Special Investigations said it had begun proceedings to revoke Kolnhofer's citizenship, charging that he concealed his identity when he immigrated to the United States in 1952.
"He never would have received a U.S. visa had he disclosed the truth," Eli Rosenbaum, director of the Office of Special Investigations, said.

Kolnhofer has worked in construction jobs in the Kansas City area, and lived at one time in Florida, according to local attorney Robert DeCoursey. He said Kolnhofer came to see him about 10 days ago about the pending Justice Department action.
DeCoursey said Kolnhofer's wife was dead and he had no children, and that he owned the home in Kansas City.

The Justice Department complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Kansas City charged Kolnhofer with taking part in Nazi atrocities while serving as an SS guard at concentration camps in Germany. It alleged that Kolnhofer joined the German Waffen-SS during the Second World War and served as an armed guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp near Berlin until January 1944.

Tens of thousands of Jews and other prisoners died at Sachsenhausen, the site of some of the most gruesome Nazi medical experiments on prisoners. The Justice Department said Kolnhofer later transfered to Buchenwald, a concentration camp near Weimar, Germany, where thousands were murdered by hanging, shooting, lethal injection and other means.

To date, 57 people with pasts involving Nazi persecution have been stripped of U.S. citizenship. A total of 49 have been removed from the United States since the Office of Special Investigations began operations in 1979. More than 300 people are currently under investigation, the Justice Department said.
